subtopic: IMMIGRATION
IMMIGRATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last April 4, the Supreme Court of Canada ruled that henceforth the Immigration Appeal Board would have to hear personally all applicants for refugee status. Following a first refusal, the future refugee could until now send his file to the Immigration Appeal Board, which reached its decisions on the basis of the transcript of an interview. From now on, all future refugees will be able to make their case in person.
Yesterday, the Deputy Minister of Employment and Immigration stated during a TV interview that a general amnesty was one of the solutions being considered to unlock the refugee status recognition process. Between 13,000 and 20,000 people are now trapped in this system.
Whether or not there is a general amnesty, I would like to point out that this should not prevent the Government from reviewing the system used for refugee status determination. In addition, everyone suspects that the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) has already received Rabbi Gunther Plaut's report but does not want to make it public. Canadian men and women are all anxiously waiting for the publication of this report, Mr. Speaker, for immigration matters are all vitally important for the future of our country.

subtopic: APARTHEID
APARTHEID
subsubtopic: CONDUCT CODE APPLICABLE TO CANADIAN COMPANIES OPERATING IN SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to speak to the House this morning regarding the Code of Conduct for Canadian companies in South Africa.
From Statistics Canada figures we know that there are 35 Canadian companies operating in South Africa, yet only 21 of the companies have been contacted by the Department of External Affairs to have the Code of Conduct communicated
to them. Only six of the companies have ever reported under the Code, and only one company continues to report, Alcan.
I believe it is inexcusable for the Government to permit a code, which it says it takes seriously, to be treated so lightly by the companies involved. We call on the Government first, to strengthen the Code as the churches task force has suggested; second, to assure that all Canadian companies in South Africa are informed about the Code; and, third, we ask the Minister to use his moral authority to see to it that all companies report under the Code.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE
ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the abortion controversy has been focused on the question of the rights for the unborn, and now it seems that the disgraceful, unacceptable treatment of the unborn has been extended to babies as well. Last fall a pregnant 19-year old high school graduate gave birth to a healthy six-pound, full-term baby girl, and subsequently left the infant to drown in a toilet bowl.
The trial took place last month. The Crown laid four charges: manslaughter, infanticide, neglecting to obtain assistance in childbirth and concealing a dead body, and finally, concealing the dead body of a child. Through the process of plea-bargaining, the Crown agreed to accept a guilty plea to the charge of concealing the body of a child, which was the lesser of the four charges. On top of this, the woman was finally given an absolute discharge, hinging primarily on the irrelevant claim that the mother did not know she was pregnant.
On behalf of all the parents who have lost a baby, or who have not been able to have one, on behalf of those who have been blessed with children, and above all, for those who recognize the sanctity and dignity of life, I would like to register my disgust and outrage that neither our political nor our legal system has taken any steps whatsoever to appeal the extremely poor judgment of the Crown prosecutor in this instance.

THE PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, every week when our constituents go to the grocery store they have to pay

subtopic: GRAND CANAL PROPOSAL
GRAND CANAL PROPOSAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, earlier this week Robert Bourassa, the Quebec Liberal Leader, in his book, Power From the North, advanced a proposal called the Grand Canal. This idea for the development and export of hydro and water resources in the James Bay area has long been a dream of a resident of St. John's, Newfoundland, Tom Kierans. The proposal would amass great quantities of water in northern Quebec and, with the aid of increased hydro power, pump it to a height where it could flow into the Great Lakes water system and, indeed, further on west.
The idea appears to have received a very favourable response in the United States from businessmen and politicians. Indeed, in Canada a number of government agencies and a number of prominent Canadians have expressed enthusiastic support. Mr. Kierans believes it will be the greatest private sector-government initiative to take place in Canada since the CPR. For me, it could also be a key to unlocking the vast hydro electric potential of Labrador.
I know there are critics and opponents of this scheme. Yet it is said that the Grand Canal will provide more clean water, reduce acid rain, improve agriculture, encourage trade with the U.S., and last, but by no means least, create hundreds of thousands of new jobs. I want to know where the Government stands on this proposal. If it supports the proposal, why has it not promoted it in the U.S.? We as Members of Parliament should ensure that there is a full analysis and assessment of this proposal by the appropriate parliamentary committee as soon as possible

subtopic: BANKS AND BANKING
BANKS AND BANKING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canadians have again been told that the Canadian Commercial Bank needs more of their money for more bailing out, to the tune of $685 million total. The Bank of Canada Governor, Gerald Bouey, yesterday promised $215 million more of public money to the CCB stating that he will put in "whatever amount of liquidity it may require". This bail-out comes from a bottomless pit. This is the new Bank of Bouey.
I note with interest that the Canadian Commercial Bank deals not with ordinary Canadian depositors but with large deposits from the chartered banks and large corporations. The press reported today that $2.7 billion of $3 billion in liabilities were in this kind of deposit. Therefore the chartered banks are not happy with the $60,000 limit which ordinary Canadians received when Pioneer Trust went under. Instead, they call on the Governor of the Bank of Canada to bail them out. This is what it means when a bank cannot fail in Canada. It has too many corporate friends with the right government connections to allow failure.
Surely we should rename the Canadian Commercial Bank the "Bank of Bouey". It operates by his fiat alone, it brings no return to the Canadian public that is supporting it, it is a testament to the public policy failure that props up the fat cats who have over-gorged themselves. And the Government totally backs this policy of public welfare for the rich.

subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE
NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on April 17, 1984, the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Nielsen) announced the phased closure of the Canadian Forces Supplementary Radio System at Inuvik, Northwest Territories. Although this had been anticipated for some time, the announcement still came as a shock to the community which will likely lose some 800 people out of a population of 3,500. The military has been an integral part of the Town of Inuvik almost since its founding, and has brought stability to an area with a precarious resource based economy. The part played by military personnel and their families in the life of the town will be long remembered in a most favourable light.
The commitment given by the Minister that he will co-operate fully with the municipal and territorial authorities to reduce the negative impact of the closure is welcomed, and the prompt action of the territorial Government, particularly that of Mr. Dan Norris, the regional director, is to be applauded.
It is essential that all government Departments work together to Find uses for the facilities to be vacated by DND. In particular, in keeping with his promise to strengthen northern defences, the Minister must utilize Inuvik to the fullest extent
April 19, 1985

in connection with the North Warning System and other military developments in northern Canada.

subtopic: FINANCE
FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) recently suggested that his budget would be inflationary and he added that wage increases would be responsible for a higher inflation rate in 1985.
I would like to point out to the House that, after the tremendous success of the six and five program, inflationary pressures have gone down in Canada and the rate of inflation has fallen from 11 and 12 per cent to 3.7 per cent, bringing down wage settlements and major collective agreements to a lower level in 1984 without affecting the purchasing power of workers.
In the private sector, the average wage increase has been 3.2 per cent, as against 3.9 per cent in the public sector, according to the figures released last March 13.
Unless this Government forgoes completely its responsibility as concerns wage policy, it is unthinkable for the Minister of Finance to accuse Canadian workers of being the main cause of inflation at this time.
Why is the Minister of Finance now saying that his budget will be inflationary? Could it be because of the additional tax on gasoline, which will have a direct and immediate impact on the consumer price index? The Minister of Finance is attempting to blame Canadian workers for an upsurge in the inflation rate which he himself will cause with his consumer tax increases.
On the other hand, the statement made by the Minister of Finance to the effect that his budget will be inflationary at a time when the wage negotiation process is in full swing can only result in even greater confusion and uncertainty for employers and employees.

subtopic: VOLUNTARY ORGANIZATIONS
VOLUNTARY ORGANIZATIONS
subsubtopic: IMPORTANCE OF WORK DONE BY VOLUNTEERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is National Volunteer Week and ceremonies and celebrations are being held in communities throughout the country to recognize the valuable contributions of volunteers. Without the countless hours of dedicated work by volunteers, the quality of
Oral Questions
life for many Canadians would be considerably diminished. When volunteers assist the poor, the disadvantaged, the sick and the aged, they make those persons feel that their problems can be overcome, that somebody does care.
Today's volunteers are often advocates of social change. Because they are so close to the communities they serve, they provide both a social conscience and a knowledgeable voice. The self-help movement in Canada has become the new wave of volunteerism. In this form of voluntary action, individuals join together in groups to support each other in dealing with problems which affect them in their daily lives.
I like to think of the example set by Lindy Fraser here in Ottawa. Her efforts to overcome a debilitating bone disease led her to start a self-help group, not only in her own city but across the country, to provide advice, support, and understanding to others facing the same disease. Her action testifies to the creative powers which can be unleashed through volunteerism. Lindy's example is particularly compelling since she was 90 years old when she set up this organization. Truly, volunteerism knows no limits. It is therefore appropriate that Hon. Members take this opportunity to recognize the vitality, strength, and importance of volunteering which is exhibited not only during National Volunteer Week but throughout the year.

Supplementary Fiscal Equalization Payments

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY FISCAL EQUALIZATION PAYMENTS 1982-87 ACT MEASURE TO ENACT

speechtext: The House resumed, from Thursday, April 18, consideration of the motion of Mrs. McDougall (for the Minister of Finance) that Bill C-39, an Act to provide for the making of supplementary fiscal equalization payments to certain provinces for the period April 1, 1982 to March 31, 1987, be now read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY FISCAL EQUALIZATION PAYMENTS 1982-87 ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to rise in the House today to speak to a Bill that, while it is very important to the country as a whole, is particularly significant because of the resulting inequity in its treatment of Quebec. Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this Bill is to provide for the making of supplementary fiscal equalization payments.
I would like to say first of all why I am opposed to the Bill, and at this point, I want to express not only my own opinion as the Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie, as a Member from Quebec, but also the views of the Government of Quebec, and I would like to recall for Hon. Members what was said by the Quebec Minister of Finance, Mr. Duhaime. I shall, if I may, give a summary of the statement made by Mr. Duhaime in the Quebec National Assembly.
First of all, Mr. Duhaime explained that the Premier of Quebec and himself had made representations to the Federal Government, urging it to provide an equitable solution to the problem created by the 1982-87 formula that will result in a drop in equalization entitlements for Quebec. The Government felt that two points were particularly important and, in fact, fundamental. First of all, Quebec could not accept the reduction in equalization entitlements for 1985-86 and 1986-87, compared with 1984-85, considering that the province does not expect any significant improvement in its economy compared with the other provinces, and the reduction thus contradicts the whole philosophy of the equalization program.
The second major point for Quebec, still according to the Quebec Minister of Finance, is that the Federal Government should consider the more general problem caused by the anticipatory aspect of the new equalization program for the five years in the period 1982-87. According to Mr. Duhaime, Quebec is the only province getting less out of the 1982-87 equalization than it would otherwise have obtained. Quebec's loss is very substantial, according to Mr. Duhaime, and was estimated at about $750 million, while the other equalization recipients were gaining a total of $445 million under the formula.
Mr. Duhaime went on to recall that during his meetings with the federal Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) he pointed out that the Federal Government's device for providing supplementary equalization payments for the year 1985-86 meant that lump sum payments would go to six provinces receiving equalization, namely, $110 million to Quebec, $50 million to Manitoba, $20 million to Nova Scotia, $20 million to New Brunswick, $15 million to Newfoundland and $5 million to Prince Edward Island. In 1986-87, no payments will be made except to Manitoba which will receive $65 million. Thus, all provinces receiving equalization payments will share $285 million over the next two years. Out of that amount, a sum of $175 million, according to Mr. Duhaime, is being added to the $445 million already received, making a grand total of $620 million for the Atlantic Provinces and Manitoba. At the same time, Quebec's loss of $750 million, under the new formula, is being corrected, but only very partially, by a payment of $110 million for 1985-86, leaving Quebec with a net loss of $640 million. Mr. Duhaime went on to say that, in his discussions with the federal Government, he had given due consideration to the federal Government's precarious financial and budgetary situation. I think that the Government of Quebec, particularly the Minister of Finance, and the Premier of Quebec did show restraint in this case since the Government of Quebec agreed to reduce its initial request for $750 million to $450 million, $300 million in 1985-86 and $150 million in 1986-87. According to Mr. Duhaime, however, the unilateral and political settlement announced by the federal Minister of Finance is far from satisfactory, it is even beyond comprehension.
Mr. Duhaime pointed out that, under the solution advocated by the federal Government, Quebec's equalization rights this year will be close to $200 million less than last year's. He stated: "I am surprised and astonished, but I see no logic in the proposed settlement. It allocates funds to some provinces which, according to the federal Government's own forecasts, do not stand to lose any equalization rights in 1985-86 and which are already favourably dealt with as a result of changes to the 1982 equalization program." Be that as it may, Mr. Duhaime said that the file remains open as far as the Quebec Government is concerned, and that they are waiting for further discussions with federal officials with a view to obtaining fair and equitable compensation based on the very principle of equalization rather than on unilateral policy as stated, unfortunately, by the Minister of Finance of this federal Government.
Mr. Speaker, it is easy to understand what is going on. I think that all Members of the House, particularly Quebec Members, have received a document from the Quebec Minister of Finance. All explanations in the file were crystal clear. Yesterday I showed the Hon. Member for LaSalle (Mr. Lanthier) one of the documents contained in the file of the Minister of Finance, and I dare hope that all Quebec Members
April 19, 1985

will look over the chart showing that the Province of Newfoundland, which had not incurred any losses, was given a $15 million gift on the eve of the election. As we all know, they have a Conservative Government. Prince Edward Island had a loss of $5 million and got $5 million, Nova Scotia lost $50 million and got $20 million, New Brunswick-another province headed by a Conservative Government, no losses, according to the federal Government-received a $20 million gift so Mr. Hatfield might spruce up his image. As to Manitoba, a loss of $72 million last year, a gain of $50 million this year and $65 million more next year.
I would suggest that the Members from Quebec would be well advised to examine the Quebec figures in the document sent by the Minister of Finance. Quebec has a loss of $750 million but gets only $110 million. Why did the Government fail to react positively to the proposal or suggestion made yesterday by the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau), the compromise offered by the former Liberal Government? Interim compensation over the next two years would have enabled Quebec to get the same amount as before, it would not have been penalized. In the meantime, the federal Government could have had discussions with Quebec with respect to such contentious issues as population figures and the overall total. In my opinion, Members of the Quebec caucus could have been wiser, and I hope they will be on the ball and raise the issue at next week's caucus and urge the Minister of Finance to maintain the transitional payment formula for the next two years. Why did he not do it for Quebec, and why not do it now? Second, why this attempt to push the Bill through? Why does the Minister of Finance want to give us that hand-out? I was disappointed yesterday when it was a Member from Quebec, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance and Member for LaSalle (Mr. Lanthier), who said: That is all we have. We must therefore try to find out who is telling the truth in that party opposite. In a statement made in public at a press conference, following a meeting with the Premiers where the Quebec Finance Minister was also present, the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mul-roney) said that the door was still open and that negotiations were still possible even though the Minister of Finance had closed that door. We do not have to take the Minister at his word however because it is often possible to have him change his mind. In any case, I trust that the Prime Minister himself can keep his word, otherwise, everyone will know that he cannot.
If the Prime Minister said that he was willing to resume negociations with Quebec, why are they in such a hurry to pass this Bill? Why not wait? Would it not have been wiser for the Quebec Premier to meet with the Prime Minister of Canada, as the Prime Minister was willing to do, and review this file and at least listen to what Quebec had to say and make the necessary changes?
Supplementary Fiscal Equalization Payments
I presume all Quebec Members have seen in the newspapers the headline "Equalization: Duhaime will keep after the Quebec Conservatives". He helped you during the last campaign, but I will say he is beginning to regret it.
"Wilson: Quebec must recognize that the Federal Government could not do any better in the present situation." The Parliamentary Secretary and the Minister of Finance keep talking about the deficit, but it was not the same tune when it was time to negotiate $2.5 billion for the West. I can see the Minister of State for Transport (Mr. Bouchard), who carries the luggage for the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) and who is saying that all this is not serious as far as Quebec is concerned. I can hardly wait to see him rise and speak for Quebec.
I have here another article entitled "Equalization: Ottawa is willing to listen". Are the Prime Minister's statements made at press conferences mere rhetoric? Or mere bluffing? "Mul-roney is willing to re-open the equalization debate on a more comprehensive level." This means that what the Prime Minister said was untrue because, today, his Party is trying anxiously to get this Bill through post haste and in an underhanded manner without continuing to negotiate.
But Duhaime is not cringing! At least, he has guts. He could inspire others. According to Jean-Louis Roy, this is a flawed compromise as far as equalization is concerned.
Mr. Speaker, I think it would be helpful and wise... Normally, when you are right in the middle of negotiations, and I believe that any ordinary Canadian will agree, when a tenant and a landlord are negotiating a rent or lease, the landlord does not write out the lease forthwith, but waits until negotiations and discussions are over. But now the Government is trying to impose this. Have any pressures been applied by Ontario or Western Members, since the Quebec Members in the Party opposite all seem to be sound asleep? This Bill will be passed quickly and the money will go elsewhere. I do not know about that. Well, then it is not too bad.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to speak briefly to Bill C-39, a Bill introduced by the Government to provide for the making of supplementary fiscal equalization payments to certain provinces for the period from 1982 to 1987. First of all, I would like to say that our Party thinks the Bill is unfair to the Province of Quebec. In fact, that is why a number of my colleagues have spoken out quite vigorously on the subject.
Of course, I could enumerate the payments that will be made to the various provinces, but since this information is already on the record, I would rather elaborate on the specific
April 19, 1985

case of Quebec which I feel is getting very little in the way of equalization payments under the new formula since the new Conservative Members from Quebec seem reluctant to comment at all, being content to praise and approve the Government's proposal. Mr. Speaker, Quebec's loss has been estimated at about $750 million, while other provinces are actually receiving payments totalling about $445 million. When I said $750 million, these are the very figures used by the Quebec Minister of Finance. Our Party cannot support this legislation, not because it gives money to the provinces, Mr. Speaker, but because we believe it does not give enough and is in fact unconstitutional. Last Wednesday, the Prime Minister spoke about equality. We are far from this equality enshrined in Section 36 of the 1982 Constitutional Act, which says the following about equalization and regional disparities:
36(1) Without altering the legislative authority of Parliament or of the provincial legislatures, or the rights of any of them with respect to the exercise of their legislative authority. Parliament and the legislatures, together with the government of Canada and the provincial governments, are committed to:
And then there are three commitments:
(a)	promoting equal opportunities for the well-being of Canadians;
(b)	furthering economic development to reduce disparity in opportunities; and
(c)	providing essential public services of reasonable quality to all Canadians.
Of course, these three commitments in the Canadian Constitution underlie the whole equalization system in Canada. For my part, Mr. Speaker, I find this Bill unacceptable because it does not completely satisfy the three conditions I have just mentioned. Under the present formula, Quebec's equalization entitlement will probably be $200 million below the level of the payments for the last fiscal year.
On the one hand, amounts are being allocated to provinces which had already benefited from the changes made to the equalization program in 1982, and, on the other hand, a large portion is being taken away from Quebec, which seems to be the only province that has to pay for what I would call a poor decision made by the Conservative Government. This is a political decision considering which provinces will be losing. We have Quebec, on the one hand, led by a Parti Quebecois Government, and not by a Conservative Government, and Manitoba on the other hand, which has also rejected the Conservative Party and elected a New Democrat Government. By accident, these are the only two provinces to lose out in the little game of equalization.
In my opinion, what should take place at this time is a public review of the equalization system rather than under the table negotiations with selected governments to quieten those that make too much noise and keep the friends of the Government happy.
As it was said in this House, some people want to blame the previous Government for the current equalisation formula. Moreover, they want to do this while ignoring the economic situation. You will recall that, when the previous equalization program was established in 1981, very few Canadians could have forecast the economic problems that would befall
Supplementary Fiscal Equalization Payments Canada. Naturally, because of this economic situation, certain provinces did not receive as much money. Today, blaming the former Government is easy but at the time the legislation was passed in this House, no one could forecast that the years 1982 and 1983 would be disastrous economically, not only in Canada, but throughout the world. Yet, the agreement reached in 1981 was signed in good faith by a responsible Government. If it is felt that the time has come to review the agreement, let us do so! Indeed, by looking at the agreement and making certain changes, the Conservative Government could have been more generous. If it decided not to do so, it is its own decision and its own responsibility, and it seems to me that it would be difficult at this time to blame the previous Government, which is the strategy regularly used by this Government to extract itself from the difficulties it gets into from time to time.
My comments will be brief. I shall simply and unhesitatingly say that a Liberal Government under the present Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) and advised by some of us, especially by my colleague from Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Gar-neau), would have been a lot more generous than the Conservative Government has been to the Province of Quebec, and would also have been a lot more respectful of the rights of all the Provinces in providing their citizens with equal and equitable education and health services.
Where are the Conservative Members of Parliament when we speak about equalization and the punitive way in which this Government has treated Quebec? No one can say that they have been very forceful. I hope that they will have the courage to take more solid positions and to defend Quebec instead of approving their Minister of Finance, who is unfortunately trying to solve his deficit problems at the expense of Quebecers, and partly at the expense of Manitobans.
Mr. Speaker, I have tried to briefly explain to you the reasons why we, on this side of the House, find it difficult to support this Government bill, a bill which we would be pleased to support if the amounts allocated, in particular to the Province of Quebec, were more generous. So, when the question is put and you see us oppose this bill, you should not conclude that the Liberal Party of Canada does not want that additional funding to be given to Quebec; on the contrary, we find that the increase granted to Quebec is not enough.

I say that because of the actual and true intent of equalization payments. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to conclude my remarks on the Bill before the House today, an Act to provide for the making of supplementary fiscal equalization payments to certain provinces for the period April 1, 1982 to March 31, 1987.
Before we adjourned for lunch, I was making the point that the actual intention of equalization payments was to provide help to lower income provinces to make it possible for them, along with their local governments, to provide reasonably comparable levels of public services at reasonably comparable levels of taxation. When we talk about public services, normally in high unemployment areas we immediately think about infrastructure in the form of water systems, sewer systems and roads. These are the very areas where there are incredible discrepancies in levels of service across the country. In the case of my Province of Newfoundland, about $600 million or $700 million this year will be passed over in the form of unconditional grants to the Government of Newfoundland to provide comparable levels of public services to those existing in other provinces. Of course the "have" provinces have the taxation base from which to be able to provide those services to the general public.
When we total all the equalization payments over the past few years, we arrive at an incredible figure. That money was supposed to go toward providing services for the general public. However, as I have pointed out to the House, there are 40 or 50 communities in my riding which do not have water systems. How could that be when the intent of these equalization payments was to correct such inadequacies? Why is it that the roads are not paved in a great portion of my riding, if the purpose of equalization payments, as the Act indicates, is to provide comparable levels of public services?
The point is that the money does not go to provide the services outlined in the Act and in the agreements. It does not go to assist communities which want water. Today, in 1985, there are school children who do not have the benefit of uncontaminated drinking water. If we ask medical doctors in certain parts of the country about major problems, of course they will talk about the inadequate quantity of drinking water. I have seen little slips from the Department of Health indicating the water is unfit for human consumption. Whenever I see a Bill such as this one coming before the Chamber, I think about the fact that this money is not used for what it was intended.
These communities try to obtain federal grants which are available. I suppose they will be available next year after the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) has his say in the Budget and after the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) decides what she will do as far as short-term job-creation programs are concerned. The majority of this money should be spent on providing water and essential services to small, isolated communities.
As far as the intention of the Government is concerned, we need only look at the publication entitled A New Direction for Canada to find the implementation of the strategy on page 84, where the following is indicated quite clearly:
To achieve the target will necessitate a careful examination of all federal expenditures-economic and regional development, social programs, federal-provincial transfers,... to develop an orderly plan to slow their growth-
That is the intention of the Government. The Government will not increase expenditures over a period of time. There will not be the same level of increases we have seen over the years. It will slow the growth of these payments. It then says, "while reshaping their composition to minimize the effects of contraction on the economy". I would suggest that one of the measures the Government should take if it is going to cut back on these payments to the provinces is to ask the provinces to be accountable for where that money goes. In other words, if it is the intent of legislation to provide public services in a province that are comparable to public services in other provinces in Canada, then that provincial Government should have to indicate where the money went. That seems only logical.
It is fine to talk about equalization payments and about how much more money will go to provincial Governments. The Premier of Newfoundland has said that under this Government, we are receiving increased equalization payments. The Government of Newfoundland has received increased equalization payments every single year. The fact of the matter is that the formula is rather unfair. We are being told Newfoundland is going to be a rich province because of all the offshore oil out there. The fact of the matter is that energy revenues mean a reduction in equalization dollar for dollar.
The new Government indicated that for the first five years of oil production in Newfoundland, the diminishing return on equalization payments will be slowed down. If the provincial treasury were to get $10 per barrel on a billion barrels of oil, it would receive $10 billion over a period of 20 years, the time it will take for the offshore oil to be developed. When talking about equalization payments, $10 billion is peanuts. The province is already getting $700 million per year over 20 years, and that would come to much more than the revenue that would be received from the oil. The point is that in the case of the Province of Newfoundland as it relates to equalization payments, we should ask why the money is not being used to provide the services that are supposed to be provided.
If we were only discussing money and if the entire offshore accord with the Province of Newfoundland meant money and only money, we would have to come to the conclusion that under this particular piece of legislation Newfoundland ends up with zero. When the province makes money from energy, it loses on equalization payments.
The so-called poor provinces should be looking at a change of direction in provincial Government policy regarding the utilization of the money provincial Governments receive. We should ask what we can do to foster industrial development so we will then have a tax base and will not need to receive
April 19, 1985

equalization payments. Why was that not considered when the offshore oil agreement was signed? Why did the agreement contain the clause that none of the oil from the offshore could come into Newfoundland to develop refineries and petrochemical industries there but rather that it had to satisfy the demands of the eastern Canadian refining and industrial capacity? In other words, the agreement was all about money going to the provincial treasury. It was about an amount of money that is not as great as the equalization payments would be over the life of the development.
In conclusion-

When block funding came into the Province of Newfoundland, the provincial Government froze the development of all senior citizens' homes and nursing homes in the province. They put the matter under study for four years. That payment is made on a per capita basis and has a built-in escalation. Therefore, money was going into the provincial treasury for the purpose of providing 75 per cent of the cost of the retirement of the debt on senior citizens' homes and nursing homes after individuals had paid and CMHC had brought the mortgage rate down to 2 per cent. That amount of money was increasing every year but no senior citizens' or nursing homes were being built until the matter was studied for three or four years. Where did that extra money go? It certainly did not go to senior citizens' homes and nursing homes.
When looking at the financial papers of these senior citizens' and nursing homes, one begins to realize that every time the Minister of Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) announces an increase in the old age pension, no one who lives in a senior citizens' or nursing home in this country sees that increase. We see what happens when a provincial administration is given a bunch of money with no strings attached other than a general intent to increase the level of public services. Some provincial Governments will spend the money where it is supposed to be spent but a great many of them will not do so. In fact, when examining the expenditures of the Government of Newfoundland, we can see where waste exists and where the Government has not been following through on the intended use of the money that was being transferred.
It is indeed unfortunate that when looking at the formula that controls this Bill, one must realize that the bottom line is zero in certain administrations. The bottom line is zero as it relates to Hibernia. The bottom line is zero as it relates to the Government of Newfoundland. The bottom line would not have been zero if there had not been the clause in the agreement indicating that the offshore oil would be used to

Mr. Speaker, 1 am pleased to speak briefly on Bill C-39. I would like to begin by congratulating my colleague from Gander-Twillin-gate (Mr. Baker) for his eloquent remarks. I hesitated in rising to speak this afternoon because I wanted to give the Conservative back-benchers from the Province of Quebec an opportunity to speak.

Although 1 waited for a few moments, Mr. Speaker, 1 failed to see the Hon. Member from Duvernay (Mr. Della Noce) and other Hon. Members rise to speak on behalf of their constituents and ask the very questions they should have raised in the House this afternoon. I must say that 1 am somewhat disappointed, because I was looking forward to hearing the Hon. Member for Duvernay who undoubtedly would have made a very eloquent speech, perhaps he will choose to do so when 1 am finished.
Mr. Speaker, when discussing fiscal equalization payments, we should remember the promises that were made to the Canadian people last fall.

When the Conservative Government was elected last fall, I do not recall that it said it would short-change the Province of Quebec or any other province, not even the Province of Ontario, which also qualifies for equalization payments. The Province of Ontario should not qualify for equalization payments, but it has been so poorly run over the last number of years that it is in the situation in which it does qualify. The Province of Ontario definitely needs a change.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) will be campaigning in Ontario for the next few days to give a hand to Premier Miller. Perhaps the Prime Minister is right in doing that because the Premier needs all the help he can get. As the Minister of State for Fitness and Amateur Sport (Mr. Jelinek) is from Ontario, he will know that the Premier's campaign is flat and that he is not doing very well. The Prime Minister is setting a precedent in helping the Premier, and I hope that he will campaign on the same theme on which he campaigned last August-time for a change. It would be nice to hear the Prime Minister say that during the election campaign in Ontario. Perhaps he could also raise the issue of equalization payments and indicate that the Province of Ontario has been so poorly run over the last number of years that it now qualifies for those payments. But the province will not take the equalization payments because that would indicate that it is not in as good a financial situation as it was before, and Ontario Tories would never admit to their shortcomings. That would be admitting that a change is needed in Toronto. Of course, we all know that a change is needed. I hope that the Prime Minister will campaign on the same theme as he did last summer and say that it is time for a change. After 43 years, it is time for a change.
Why is it that we are a little short right now in providing the provinces with the payments which they need? There may be several reasons. The Government spends 80 per cent to 90 per
cent of its time telling us that it cannot fulfil its election promises because of the previous Government. That strategy is wearing thin. The Government has been in power for eight months. Government Members seemed to have had the resources to fulfil just about anything before they were elected. They made 338 promises. However, in none of those promises did they say: "Vote for me and I will cut your payments". Perhaps it was an oversight on the part of the Government.
Let us look at the areas in which the Government has cut its funding to the provinces. Not only do we know that the Province of Quebec and others will be losing many millions of dollars worth of equalization payments because of the actions of this Government, but we also know, for example, that as a result of the cut-backs which were announced on November 8, black Thursday, the Province of Quebec will lose $770 million because of the book of cut-backs. Those are the cut-backs which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) inflicted upon the people of Canada. They range from cuts in agricultural programs to cuts in capital expenditures and construction and all kinds of other reported cuts. The cancellation of the census is even included but, of course, the Government changed its mind on that.
Incidentally, Mr. Speaker, I am sure you are aware that the information in the census was necessary in order to establish the equalization grants, to which the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Andre), who is here right now, would attest. The provinces probably shook the Minister of Finance hard. The Minister of Supply and Services must have given him a few shoves himself. And it was only because of those actions that the Minister of Finance changed his mind and reinstated the census, ensuring somewhere in the order of 6,000 full-time jobs, plus about 40,000 part-time jobs, which had been lost as a result of this particular cut-back. A vast amount of funding has been cut by the federal Government throughout those same areas of the country which are once again suffering because of the lowering of the equalization grant.
I must also take a moment to discuss what the Government is doing with the funds it has. Of course, one of the reasons it cannot provide these grants is because it is spending-or should I say "wasting"-the money elsewhere. What is it wasting its money on? Let me start by stating the fact that we have the largest Cabinet in the history of this country. It is not just 1 per cent or 2 per cent larger than we had before, not even 10 per cent larger. The Cabinet we have now, Mr. Speaker, is about 25 per cent if not 30 per cent larger, than the Cabinet of the previous Government. The population of this country did not explode by 30 per cent overnight when this Government was elected. They are the same people who were here prior to September 4. But the Conservatives, in order to run this country, needed a Cabinet which was one-third larger than the Cabinet of the Liberals. Perhaps that is because the Conservatives are only two-thirds as efficient as the Liberals and needed a larger Cabinet in order to get the same results.

There may be another reason, Mr. Speaker. Perhaps the Conservatives needed a make-work program. One would think that a make-work program would address itself to the general population. However, in the case of this Government, the make-work program really addresses itself to members of the Conservative Party who had been elected-and some who were not who needed something to do. So the book-ends, or "surfers" as we call them, those who came in with the tide, needed something to do and, of course, the Government decided to appoint a much larger than necessary Cabinet. There were 40 Cabinet Ministers. We are seeing a gradual reduction in the size of the Cabinet as Ministers resign; however, it is still a 39-member Cabinet. The other day I had a hard time getting into the parking lot with my automobile, Mr. Speaker, because a lot of limousines were blocking the entrance, waiting for Cabinet Ministers to come out of their meeting or whatever it was they were doing in the building at that particular time.

These are the people in the office who apologize and write letters of refusal for the Ministers. Of course, the Minister himself writes a letter of acceptance whenever he gives out money and the political commissars sign the letter whenever he refuses. I've had experience with that in letters I have received from Cabinet Ministers. Some of them are signed by the political commissars, but whenever a letter says "We are glad to agree with you", in most cases it is signed by the Minister.
The Government seemed to have plenty of resources when it came time to reward its own. The Government has made approximately 1200 political appointments since the election of last September. I am sure that every Conservative backbencher must be ashamed of this record, Mr. Speaker. Not only did the Government appoint 1200 people, but a large number are defeated Tory candidates. Not 1200 Tories were defeated, of course, but I will say that most of the high-paying jobs were given to defeated Conservative candidates. speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of Supply and Services) moved
subtopic: CROWN ASSETS DISPOSAL CORPORATION DISSOLUTION ACT
speechtext:
that Bill C-43, an Act to dissolve the Crown Assets Disposal Corporation and to amend the Surplus Crown Assets Act and other Acts in consequence thereof, be now read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to begin debate today on this very important legislation, especially as it is the first piece of legislation I have had the opportunity to introduce.

subtopic: CROWN ASSETS DISPOSAL CORPORATION DISSOLUTION ACT
speechtext: It is your second.

subtopic: CROWN ASSETS DISPOSAL CORPORATION DISSOLUTION ACT
speechtext:
Yes, it is my second; I stand corrected. I do not think I had a chance to debate the first one.
In any event, although this is essentially an administrative or bookkeeping Bill, it is important because it directly reflects this Government's commitment to fiscal responsibility, deficit reduction, leaner government, increased accountability and a reduced role for Crown Corporations. I will return to those points in detail in my later remarks, but first I thought it would be useful for the House to have a brief history of the Crown Assets Disposal Corporation and the events which have precipitated the introduction of this Bill today.
The Corporation was created by the Government in 1943 under the name War Assets Disposal Corporation. Its purpose was obviously to dispose of excess materiel from World War II. In wartime all kinds of materials are purchased in pursuit of the war effort, not all of which are consumed in war. Those not consumed are of course unnecessary in large part after the restoration of peace. The Corporation carried on this activity until 1949, when its name and mandate was changed by the Surplus Crown Assets Act. As the name implies, at that point the Governor in Council granted to the new corporation responsibility for disposing of all surplus Crown assets, not only those relating to the war effort. It also gave the corporation responsibility for disposing of surplus assets of foreign powers located in Canada.
Crown Assets Disposal Corporation
[DOT] (M50)
In those formative years the corporation performed its function effectively and efficiently. Unfortunately, in the 1970s I do not think that efficient and effective would be two adjectives that one would use to describe the performance of that Crown corporation. If our late colleague, Mr. Tom Cossitt, was still with us, he may have had a pretty long list of activities of the corporation of which he would wish to remind the Canadian public. Those who are interested might look at some of the questions which Mr. Cossitt put on the Order Paper in 1978 and 1979 which were never answered. However, perhaps the past should stay in the past.
In any event, Mr. Speaker, Crown Assets Disposal was not unique in that regard. There were many aspects of government performance, both within Crown corporations and otherwise, that were subject to scrutiny and probing questions by Mr. Cossitt, a great many other Members of the House, and members of the public which precipitated the establishment of a royal commission on financial management and accountability called the Lambert Commission. That commission recommended a number of quite important and profound changes to the way in which government functioned in an effort to improve accountability and financial management to save the taxpayers money and ensure that the taxpayers know how their money is being spent and their assets are being disposed of. It attempted to restore some degree of political accountability in keeping with the traditions of our parliamentary democracy.
One of the recommendations of the Lambert Commission was that the activities of Crown Assets Disposal should in fact be placed directly within the operations of government as a common service. In 1982 this occurred and the disposal activities of Crown Assets Disposal were moved into the Department of Supply and Services and have been a part of the operations of my Department ever since. It was decided that there were no advantages to retaining the arm's length relationship that a Crown corporation implies and that there would be improved accountability and responsibility and a better deal obtained for the taxpayers by having the activities conducted within government. In addition, the management and administration of the corporation was taken over by the Department of Supply and Services. These changes were implemented by Order in Council in 1982 and have been phased in. At that time all employees of Crown Assets Disposal Corporation were offered employment within the Department of Supply and Services. No one's employment was terminated outright. The vast majority of employees did accept employment with the Public Service and are so employed today.
Consequently, we have a situation in which we have a corporation in form only. There are no employees. Its activities are undertaken entirely by the employees of my Department. However, there is a legal requirement for such a corporation to exist. It must have a board of directors, hold annual meetings, produce annual reports, and maintain separate accounts which

Crown Assets Disposal Corporation must be audited. For three years we have had these unnecessary expenses carrying on.
However, as the Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria) knows, it has not been a total loss. There have been opportunities to appoint directors. Outstanding Canadians from coast to coast have been sitting on the board of directors. I'm sure the Member would know most of them personally because they were quite active in his political association. It was certainly enjoyable for them to come to Ottawa from time to time to attend annual meetings and collect a per diem. The taxpayers of Canada enjoyed the opportunity of subsidizing some very honourable and hardworking members of the Liberal Party. In October, after being sworn in as Minister, I had the sad duty of terminating some of those appointments.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: CROWN ASSETS DISPOSAL CORPORATION DISSOLUTION ACT
speechtext: Now you've got enough Tories.

subtopic: CROWN ASSETS DISPOSAL CORPORATION DISSOLUTION ACT
speechtext:
No, as a matter of fact we replaced them with public servants who reside in Ottawa and receive no per diem for attending meetings. Therefore, that expense has been cut out, but there is still the expense of maintaining separate books, producing annual reports, et cetera. This legislation is introduced to clean up that situation by removing this corporation from the books. Instead of having 438 Crown corporations we will now have 437. That is a start on the road toward reducing this unconscionably large list of structures and organizations that have been put in place over the last 20 years.
The substantial portions of Bill C-43 are dealt with in Clauses 1 to 6. I'm sure Members will have noted that Clause 5 allows any business transaction which is still in progress involving Crown Assets and outside parties to carry on. Therefore, no one will suffer personal, financial or legal consequences of these changes. The remaining 10 clauses of the Bill are consequential amendments to the Surplus Crown Assets Act and are administrative in nature. The final section is a schedule outlining consequential amendments to Acts other than the Surplus Crown Assets Act.
This is a straightforward, uncontroversial piece of legislation. For that reason I urge the House to give it speedy second reading and expeditious reference to the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates. I would like to take this opportunity to look beyond the technical aspects of this legislation and recognize its profound symbolic importance. I am deeply committed to the principle of this legislation, as is the Government. I spoke earlier of several principles which guide the Government's action.
First, the Government is committed to fiscal responsibility. Bill C-43 is fundamentally designed to eliminate duplication of effort in the Government of Canada and to formalize a process which has already saved $600,000 for the taxpayers of Canada and will result in an annual saving of that amount. In the figures we deal in around here of millions and billions, it may not seem like much, but if you look after the thousands, the millions and billions will look after themselves.
The Government is firmly committed to the principle of deficit reduction. The legislation has as its underlying premise the perpetuation and improvement of a regime which successfully recovers for the Crown some $23 million annually from surplus assets. The administration is committed to a leaner, more efficient Government. In his statement last November 8 my colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), indicated that of his four-part strategy for economic renewal one was to have less government intervention. This is one small step, but I can assure my colleagues opposite that there will be many more in the future. When the electors, or more likely old age, require us to move on, we will definitely be leaving behind a leaner, more efficient, and more effective Government than that which we inherited after 20 years of Liberal rule.
The Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens) has announced a number of very important initiatives that will attempt to clear the mess left by his predecessor. My colleague, the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret), has indicated the Government's intention to consider the privatization of a whole range of Crown corporations. Furthermore, those that will be retained for good public policy purposes will be more accountable to the House and the Canadian public and will operate in a more responsible fashion than has been the case in the past.
I have stated that accountability is the cornerstone of this Government's mandate. Therefore, we do not accept the use of the arm's length relationship of Crown corporations to avoid that accountability and responsibility. In a democratic society, we do not find reasonable and proper the previous Government's habit of removing the day to day scrutiny of activities by leaving it to the Crown corporations when those activities are part of the Government's ongoing activities. We will be increasing accountability and the responsibility of Ministers of the Government to the House on a daily basis which will be combined with the very important initiatives being recommended by the Task Force on Parliamentary Reform. This will lead to a much more democratic procedure which will assure the electors of Canada that they know what the federal Government is doing with their money and that their representatives in the House can hold the Government accountable. It is only through such change that we will begin to reverse the trend of 20 years of Liberal rule and restore a reasonable kind of Government to this country.
Although this legislation is not profound in itself, it will save money. It does establish the trend. The Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria) laughs. Much time is spent in the House worrying about appointments to directorships of Crown corporations and other positions which he believes is a concern. I suggest to him that he should be applauding loudly because we are eliminating some opportunities for such appointments through this legislation. I am making the commitment that we will continue to do so. Our Government is firmly committed to the privatization of Crown corporations when it is no longer necessary for the Government to own them. It is firmly committed to winding up those
April 19, 1985

Crown corporations that no longer serve any useful purpose. Therefore, the Hon. Member should be applauding us for removing these opportunities for political patronage.
In the meantime I can assure him, with respect to those Crown corporations that are retained for good public policy reasons, that we will continue to maintain our current practice of appointing the best people possible to those positions. He can be assured that the taxpayers and electors in his riding will be well served by the Government of Canada even though they may have chosen not to elect a representative of the right Party in the last election.
I welcome the support of my Cabinet colleagues who I know support the aims of this legislation. I urge members of the Opposition, whom I know to be thoughtful and honourable, to support this worth-while initiative.

Mr. Speaker, on behalf of my Party and as official critic I am pleased to respond to Bill C-43 which was moved by the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Andre). The Minister is slightly guilty of plagiarism in his comments. He should have at least acknowledged that the previous Government had begun the process of dismantling the Crown corporation. Of course, the Minister forgot to mention that.
The Minister's remarks left me with the impression that he was reading his address in reply to the Throne Speech rather than introducing a small, administrative Bill to eliminate a redundant corporation. Understandably, our Party is in agreement with the Bill since we had begun the process pursuant to the report of the Lambert Commission to which the Minister referred earlier. The Lambert Commission had also recommended the unification of the two arms of the Department of Supply and Services, which has already taken place as a result of the last shuffle of deputy ministers.
I was pleased to hear the Minister refer to a reduction in the number of people who are appointed through political patronage. He stated that there would be less political patronage as a result of the elimination of the board of the Crown Assets Disposal Corporation. However, I wonder if this is an indication from him that there is division within the Cabinet as far as Crown corporations are concerned because I am sure the Minister will recall that his colleague, the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Nielsen), indicated his desire to form a new Crown corporation to take over the Cyprus-Anvil Mine in the Yukon, in his riding. I am sure that difference of opinion between the Minister of Supply and Services, who wants to do away with many Crown corporations, and the Deputy Prime Minister, who wants a new Crown corporation to serve a specific interest in his riding, will eventually create a rift within the Government of Canada.
Our Party supports the dismantling process of the Crown Assets Disposal Corporation. The Minister gave us the assurance a few moments ago that no one will lose his employment as a result of this dismantling. The Minister also informed us previously that the corporation itself had very few people, if
Crown Assets Disposal Corporation
any, left on staff because it had essentially been united with the Department.
However, I want to reiterate that we believe the functions of the Crown Assets Disposal Corporation should be united with those of the Department of Supply and Services because the Minister should be in charge of all activities within his Department. We have no difficulty with this legislation, other than our wish to receive the assurance that I requested earlier.
